beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Hussain, and this video is about how A I actually helps an organization manage its data standards and its data quality. Not the dashboard version. The version where somebody has to decide what valid means, for four thousand columns, and then keep that decision true every single day while the data changes underneath them.

show.event: cream page, spark + serif greeting 'Namaste, Hussain' above an empty composer
the ask types itself into the composer, character by character
send button arms terracotta; running indicator reads 'profiling the warehouse…'
three result lines stagger in beneath — the ask lands answered

props.command: Our warehouse has 4,000 columns and 12 documented data rules. Profile the data, propose the missing rules as executable checks, rank them by what a silent failure would cost, and tell me which columns you are NOT confident enough to propose a rule for.
output: proposed 318 candidate checks, ranked by blast radius
flagged 41 columns: no rule inferable — ask an owner

beats.narration_text: Every organization already has a data quality dashboard. Ninety eight point seven percent. Green. Nobody argues with it. Here is what it is actually measuring: is the field present, and is it a string. Six spellings of one country all pass. The score is not wrong. It is measuring the wrong thing.

show.event: a big confident score card fills the frame: 98.7% QUALITY, tick, 'all checks passed'
the card lifts and goes translucent, revealing the actual column underneath it
six country values type in as rows — US, USA, U.S., United States, 'us  ', (blank) — each with a PASS chip
the six rows pull together into one bracket labelled 'one country'; the PASS chips hold
the 98.7% is struck through in terracotta; caption reads 'present is not correct'

beats.narration_text: So write more rules. That is the honest answer, and it is exactly why nobody does it. Four thousand columns. Twelve of them have a written rule. Getting one right, profiling the column, arguing the edge cases, agreeing with the owner, costs about forty minutes. That is three hundred and thirty working days to write them once. They go stale in ninety.

show.event: a dense 4,000-cell grid paints in, one cell per column, warm grey
12 cells light in ink and pull out a label: '12 columns have a written rule'
the remaining mass floods terracotta-tinted: '3,988 columns run on nobody's rule'
arithmetic strip types across the bottom: 3,988 × 40 min
the total counts up to 330 working days
a decay bar wipes back across the total: 'stale in 90'

beats.narration_text: A standard that lives in a policy document is a wish. A standard that can fail a row is a rule. Same sentence, one difference. This one names the allowed set, the scope it applies to, who owns it, and what happens when it breaks. Block the load, or let it through and warn. That is the whole art.

show.event: a policy sentence sits alone in serif: 'Country must be recorded consistently.'
it is struck through; label appears: 'a wish'
an executable expectation types in below it, line by line, in mono
each clause is annotated as it lands: allowed set · scope · owner · severity
severity token 'block' flares terracotta
a sample row drops onto the rule and is stamped FAIL; label: 'a rule'

props.sparkLine: A rule can fail a row.

beats.narration_text: So here is the ask that works. Not clean my data. That one gets you a silent rewrite you cannot audit. Profile one column. Propose the rule. Show the evidence. Name the owner. And do not change a single value.

show.event: back to the composer, empty, greeting slot reads 'The ask,'
the single-column prompt types itself in
send arms terracotta; running indicator reads 'profiling one column…'
no output lines yet — the result is the next beat (ASK then RESULT)

props.command: Profile customers.country. Propose one executable expectation with a severity and an owner. Show the evidence: value counts, the long tail, and how many rows would newly fail. Do not modify a single value.

beats.narration_text: And this comes back. Six spellings, ranked, with counts. The proposed rule underneath it. And the number that matters most: one thousand two hundred and eighty four rows would newly fail. That is not a bug report. That is a negotiation opening. Is this a data problem, or is my rule too strict?

show.event: a value-count bar chart grows to value, longest bar first: US 61%
the long tail fills in beneath — USA 22%, United States 9%, U.S. 5%, blank 3%
the proposed expectation card slides up from the bottom, already written
a counter spins up to 1,284 and holds in terracotta: 'rows would newly fail (39%)'
a question stamps beside it: 'bad data, or bad rule?'

props.proposal: expect country_code in ISO_3166_1_ALPHA_2 · severity: block · owner: crm-team
props.question: bad data, or bad rule?

beats.narration_text: This is the part that gets skipped, and it is the part that makes the whole thing work. Every proposal stops at a human. Two hundred and eighteen ratified. Fifty nine bounced to an owner who actually knows the domain. Forty one rejected, because the model pattern matched a rule the business does not have. The model proposes. People ratify.

show.event: 318 small proposal cards stream in from the left toward a terracotta gate bar
the gate holds them; an 'owner review' chip sits on the bar
the stream sorts into three lanes as each card is stamped
lane counters count up: RATIFIED 218 · NEEDS OWNER 59 · REJECTED 41
footer line lands: 'the model proposes · people ratify'

lanes.label: REJECTED
lanes.note: a rule the business never had

beats.narration_text: Then the rules stop being a document. They run on every load. A row that fails a blocking rule never reaches the warehouse. It goes to quarantine, carrying the rule that caught it and the person who owns it. The dashboard stops being a score you look at. It becomes a queue somebody works.

show.event: source node on the left, warehouse node on the right, a checks gate between them
a batch of row-dots flows left to right and enters the gate
most dots pass through to the warehouse and settle
a terracotta branch peels downward: failing dots divert to QUARANTINE
each quarantined dot grows a tag: the rule id and the owner
the label under the box flips from 'a score you look at' to 'a queue somebody works'

beats.narration_text: Three ways this goes wrong. One. Let it auto correct, and you have inherited a silent edit nobody can trace. Two. Every value can be valid and still be meaningless. A column of perfect dates that are all the load date passes everything. Three. Rules rot. The business changed. The check did not.

show.event: three empty slots wait across the frame, numbered 01 02 03
card one rises: a value silently rewritten, its original greyed out and gone; tag 'no trace'
card two rises: a column of identical dates, every row stamped VALID; tag 'valid, meaningless'
card three rises: a rule greying as a calendar advances; tag 'the check did not'
one terracotta underline lands on card three — the one that gets you

cards.title: Auto-correct
cards.body: A value rewritten in place is an edit nobody can trace back.

cards.title: Valid ≠ meaningful
cards.body: A column of perfect dates that are all the load date passes every check.

cards.title: Rules rot
cards.body: The business changed its definition. The expectation kept passing.

beats.narration_text: Let us recap. The dashboard was never measuring meaning. It was measuring presence and type. A I's real contribution is not cleaning values, it is proposing and maintaining the rules, with the evidence attached. Every proposal still stops at a human owner. And the test for all of it: can this rule fail a row, and does that failure reach a person?

show.event: the Claude artifact page opens, titled 'The Rule, Not The Report — one page'
four verdict lines stagger in, one per spoken clause
the last line holds alone — the test

props.artifactTitle: The Rule, Not The Report — one page
props.artifactHeading: What AI is actually for here
artifactLines: The dashboard measured presence and type. It never measured meaning.
AI's job is not cleaning values — it is proposing, evidencing and maintaining the rules.
Every proposal stops at a human owner. The model proposes; people ratify.
The test: can this rule fail a row, and does that failure reach a person?

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take one table you actually own, and paste this. For each column, propose one executable expectation with a severity and an owner, rank them by what a silent failure would cost, and list every column where you cannot infer a rule and must ask a human. Watch that last list hardest. The columns it refuses to guess on are the ones your organization never actually decided.

show.event: composer returns, greeting fixed to 'Your turn.'
the suggested prompt types in as the narration reads it aloud, word for word
the final clause — 'must ask a human' — lands as the voice reaches it
running indicator reads 'paste this into Claude…'; the frame holds for the pause

props.command: Here is the schema and a 1,000-row sample of one table I own. For each column, propose one executable expectation with a severity and an owner, rank them by what a silent failure would cost, and list every column where you cannot infer a rule and must ask a human. Do not modify any values.

beats.narration_text: The rule, not the report. If this changed how you will look at your next quality dashboard, subscribe. I am Hussain. Thanks for watching.

show.event: cream page, the title restates poster-style in serif with a terracotta period
the handle fades in beneath it
subline settles: 'fix the field, not the report'
